grammar.title: A gesture described as almost doing something
grammar.formation: Negative verb stem (remove ない) + んばかりに + predicate; + んばかりの + noun; + んばかりだ. する → せんばかり.
grammar.explanation: This expressive description presents an appearance close to an action, often figuratively. 言わんばかりの眼差し describes a look as if it said something; it does not report a spoken quotation. に connects the description to an action, while の attaches it to a noun. It fits narration or a deliberately expressive recollection more readily than every ordinary turn. Usually describe an observed scene; do not turn it into a claim that you know someone’s actual thoughts.
grammar.example: 彼は「まだ待って」と言わんばかりに手を振った。
grammar.translation: He waved his hand as if to say, “Wait a little longer.”

examples.ja: {彼|かれ}は「まだ{待|ま}って」と{言|い}わんばかりに{手|て}を{振|ふ}った。
examples.en: He waved his hand as if to say, “Wait a little longer.”

examples.ja: {窓|まど}の{外|そと}には{溢|あふ}れんばかりの{光|ひかり}が{広|ひろ}がっていた。
examples.en: Outside the window, light seemed to overflow.

examples.ja: {娘|むすめ}は{跳|と}び{上|あ}がらんばかりに{喜|よろこ}んだ。
examples.en: The daughter was so delighted she looked ready to jump for joy.

grammar.mistake: Remove ない before adding ん; する uses せん, not しん. A narrated appearance does not establish that the action actually happened.

grammar.title: An obstacle does not stop the action
grammar.formation: Obstacle noun + をものともせず（に） + an action continued despite it.
grammar.explanation: The expression gives the action a determined, often admiring or dramatic tone: a person keeps going despite an obstacle. It is stronger than simply saying there was difficulty. Here friends quote a storm scene from a story, then talk normally about what the character did. Do not read the phrase alone as proof that the action succeeded. The original fiction gives the concrete result separately.
grammar.example: 彼女は反対をものともせず、原稿を書き続けた。
grammar.translation: She kept writing her manuscript despite the opposition.

examples.ja: {彼女|かのじょ}は{反対|はんたい}をものともせず、{原稿|げんこう}を{書|か}き{続|つづ}けた。
examples.en: She kept writing her manuscript despite the opposition.

examples.ja: {主人公|しゅじんこう}は{寒|さむ}さをものともせず、{橋|はし}まで{歩|ある}いた。
examples.en: The protagonist walked as far as the bridge despite the cold.

examples.ja: {彼|かれ}は{何度|なんど}もの{失敗|しっぱい}をものともせずに{練習|れんしゅう}を{続|つづ}けた。
examples.en: He kept practicing despite repeated failures.

grammar.mistake: Use a noun naming the obstacle. The narrator gives the viewpoint; the following clauses establish the action and result.

grammar.title: A valued quality tied to its particular source
grammar.formation: Noun + ならではの + noun; Noun + ならではだ when the quality is already identified.
grammar.explanation: This presents something as a characteristic or distinctive strength of that person, material or experience, commonly with appreciative evaluation. In this unit, 手書きならではの味わい is the writer’s response to marks on a fictional letter. It does not claim that every handwritten work is superior to a screen, or that a geographic feature cannot exist elsewhere. The noun after の names the valued quality.
grammar.example: この短い息継ぎは、彼女ならではの工夫だ。
grammar.translation: This brief pause is a touch characteristic of her writing.

examples.ja: この{短|みじか}い{息継|いきつ}ぎは、{彼女|かのじょ}ならではの{工夫|くふう}だ。
examples.en: This brief pause is a touch characteristic of her writing.

examples.ja: {紙|かみ}ならではの{手触|てざわ}りを{楽|たの}しんだ。
examples.en: I enjoyed the distinctive feel of paper.

examples.ja: この{声|こえ}の{響|ひび}きは、{地元|じもと}の{劇団|げきだん}ならではだ。
examples.en: This resonance of voices is characteristic of the local theatre group.

grammar.mistake: Use の before the following noun. Evaluate the particular quality in context; do not treat an appreciative phrase as factual proof of exclusivity.

grammar.title: Not even one: a strong negative boundary
grammar.formation: One + counter / a minimal quantity + たりとも + negative or prohibition. Examples: 一字たりとも消さない; 一瞬たりとも忘れない.
grammar.explanation: This strongly excludes even the smallest named amount. It is formal or deliberately emphatic, rather than an everyday replacement for every も. The editor’s 一字たりとも消さない expresses a vow about an original letter; it is not a ban on revising the new story. The following predicate supplies the negative boundary. Do not confuse this with the action-listing たり…たりする pattern.
grammar.example: その便りは一字たりとも消さない。
grammar.translation: I won’t erase even a single character of that letter.

examples.ja: その{便|たよ}りは{一字|いちじ}たりとも{消|け}さない。
examples.en: I won’t erase even a single character of that letter.

examples.ja: {一瞬|いっしゅん}たりとも{無駄|むだ}にしたくない。
examples.en: I don’t want to waste even a moment.

examples.ja: {預|あず}かった{原稿|げんこう}は{一枚|いちまい}たりとも{失|うしな}わない。
examples.en: I won’t lose even one page of the manuscript entrusted to me.

grammar.mistake: Keep the negative or prohibition that gives the taught pattern its meaning. A quoted vow about one document does not automatically apply to another.

grammar: a quoted expressive description versus an actual spoken line
minimal quantity with a negative predicate
watch.prompt: Optionally listen to a short narration you already have. Note whether a quoted line was spoken or only suggested, what the character actually did, and one expressive phrase. No media upload or independent comprehension score is required.

recycling.reason: The first N1 literary unit reuses only actual recent events: Bao’s Friday offer follows the pending interview and next month starts with training. Handwritten material and ordinary friend conversation are not padded with job/slang/dialect headwords.

exercises.prompt: When does the daughter read the letter?
options: The next morning, after returning to the seaside house
At the doorway before she leaves
While running across the bridge
exercises.explain: Hana says 翌朝, and Ren checks that she has not read it on the rainy night.

exercises.prompt: What first confuses Ren about the doorway scene?
options: He thinks the daughter cannot see the light
He thinks the father shouted a line that was only suggested by a gesture
He thinks the father has read the daughter’s letter
exercises.explain: Ren rereads because he takes 行くな as a shout. Hana says 叫んでない and explains the appearance.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase does Hana consider keeping to make the viewpoint clear?
options: {父|ちち}は{全|すべ}て{説明|せつめい}した
{便|たよ}りはすでに{届|とど}いた
{娘|むすめ}にはそう{見|み}えた
exercises.explain: It identifies how the daughter sees the gesture, rather than reporting the father’s spoken words.

exercises.prompt: Complete the adverbial attachment describing how he waved.
exercises.line: {彼|かれ}は「{待|ま}って」と{言|い}わんばかり＿＿{手|て}を{振|ふ}った。
options: に
の
だ
exercises.explain: に links the expressive appearance to the action 手を振った. の needs a following noun.

exercises.prompt: Choose the modifier for the noun 光景: “a scene that seems to overflow with light.”
exercises.line: {光|ひかり}が{溢|あふ}れんばかり＿＿{光景|こうけい}
options: に
の
だ
exercises.explain: The immediate noun needs の. This is an explicit attachment task, not a choice between multiple valid full descriptions.

exercises.prompt: What does this narrated description establish?
exercises.line: {彼|かれ}は「{帰|かえ}って」と{言|い}わんばかりの{眼差|まなざ}しを{向|む}けた。
options: The exact words 帰って were definitely spoken aloud
The listener definitely went home
The narrator describes a look as if it conveyed “Go home”
exercises.explain: The described appearance neither establishes an audible quotation nor the other person’s subsequent action.

exercises.prompt: What does the daughter do before crossing?
options: Wait for the wind to ease and check her footing
Run without looking at the boards
Read the letter aloud to Misaki
exercises.explain: Hana says she stops before the bridge, waits, and watches her footing. The strong phrase does not erase those actions.

exercises.prompt: Why can the writing still be read the next morning?
options: The letter is rewritten on a phone
The daughter wraps the paper bag in a clear bag
The father replaces it with a printed copy
exercises.explain: Hana describes the extra bag, and Misaki links it to the writing remaining readable.

exercises.prompt: Choose the supplied obstacle expression before the continued action.
exercises.line: {反対|はんたい}＿＿、{彼女|かのじょ}は{書|か}き{続|つづ}けた。
options: をものともして
がものともせず
をものともせず
exercises.explain: Noun + をものともせず connects the named obstacle to the action that goes on despite it.

exercises.prompt: Build the supplied appreciative description of handwriting.
exercises.meaning: There is a distinctive handwritten charm.
exercises.explain: The source noun precedes ならではの and the valued quality follows it. This constrained target is not the only possible compliment.

exercises.prompt: Why does the daughter head back to the house?
options: To think again about her hurry in the light of the house
To return an unwanted letter and leave immediately
To ask the father to write an address before she can travel
exercises.explain: The bridge paragraph distinguishes returning the letter from returning to think again about what she was rushing towards.

exercises.prompt: What does the letter offer the daughter?
options: A fixed destination and departure day
A place she can return to if she has trouble
An order that she must never leave the house
exercises.explain: The morning paragraph says it is not a letter deciding where she must go; it tells her there is a place to come back to.

exercises.prompt: Which change occurs between the first doorway scene and the final window scene?
options: The father finally shouts 行くな
The departure date becomes fixed
The daughter responds with a wave and a spoken question
exercises.explain: She opens the window, waves back and asks about breakfast. Departure is still undecided.

exercises.prompt: What new work arrangement does Bao describe?
options: An offer received on Friday, entry next month, and a month of training
An unresolved result due after the booklet is printed
A department-head appointment without training
exercises.explain: This later scene explicitly confirms Friday’s offer and next month’s entry; it does not rewrite the earlier interview’s pending status.

exercises.prompt: Which document is covered by Ren’s “not even one character” remark?
options: Every draft Hana will ever write
The father’s letter inside the story
Bao’s job application
exercises.explain: Hana identifies the fictional father’s letter and then agrees to shorten the new explanatory paragraph.

exercises.prompt: Complete the strong negative vow about the entrusted manuscript.
exercises.line: {預|あず}かった{原稿|げんこう}は{一枚|いちまい}たりとも＿＿。
options: {失|うしな}う
{失|うしな}いたい
{失|うしな}わない
exercises.explain: The negative predicate gives this minimum-unit vow its meaning. Losing it and wanting to lose it contradict the stated vow.

exercises.prompt: Why does Hana keep 娘にはそう見えた?
options: To show the daughter’s viewpoint without revealing the father’s message early
To establish that the father shouted the exact words
To move the letter-reading scene to the beginning
exercises.explain: The second paragraph explains viewpoint and the order in which the letter’s words reach both daughter and reader.

exercises.prompt: How does the writer treat paper and screen readers?
options: She makes all handwriting identical and uses a very pale colour
She keeps varied lettering and clear lines readable for both
She denies that anyone reads on screens
exercises.explain: The material paragraph separates enjoyment of materials from making the lettering readable; it explicitly considers screen readers.

exercises.prompt: What is done with the words removed from the new draft?
options: They are erased from the fictional father’s letter
They are sent as Bao’s interview answer
They are kept on another sheet for a later draft
exercises.explain: The writer records the removed words separately; preserving the letter and revising the surrounding draft are different decisions.

exercises.prompt: Which feedback does Hana plan to ask for at the meetup?
options: Where readers took a breath or reread, and what they waited for before the letter opened
Only the colour of the paper, without reading aloud
A vote to forbid any further editing
exercises.explain: The closing paragraph asks about concrete reading behaviour rather than relying only on a broad 分かった response.
